nodes.title: AWS Lambda: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Lambda runs your code in response to events (API call, S3 upload, EventBridge schedule, SQS message). No servers to manage. You pay for invocations and execution time. The exam tests limits, cold starts, triggers, and the IAM execution role.

flashcards.front: Lambda execution limits — memory, time, payload?
flashcards.back: Memory: 128 MB - 10 GB (CPU scales with memory). Timeout: max 15 minutes. Sync invocation payload: 6 MB. Async invocation payload: 256 KB. Deployment package (zipped): 50 MB direct upload, 250 MB via S3, 10 GB via container image.

flashcards.front: Cold start — what is it and how do you minimize it?
flashcards.back: First invocation of an idle function takes 100 ms - 2 s extra to load the runtime and your code. Mitigations: provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed instances), smaller deployment packages, native-compiled runtimes (Go, Rust), keeping connections out of the handler so they're reused across invocations.

flashcards.front: Sync vs async vs poll-based invocation.
flashcards.back: Sync (API Gateway, ALB): caller waits for result. Async (S3, SNS, EventBridge): Lambda queues and retries on failure. Poll-based (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams): Lambda pulls records, processes in batches, manages retries via the source. Each has different retry semantics — read the docs.

flashcards.front: How does Lambda get permissions to call other AWS services?
flashcards.back: Each function has an IAM execution role. The role's policies say what the function CAN do (read S3, write DynamoDB, decrypt KMS). Lambda assumes the role on every invocation and exposes temporary credentials to your code via the SDK.

questions.q: A developer is building a Lambda function that processes S3 events. The function runs for 8 minutes and requires 3 GB of memory. After deployment, all invocations fail with a timeout error. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: 3 GB exceeds the maximum Lambda memory allocation
Lambda functions cannot process S3 events directly
S3 event notifications require an SQS queue as an intermediary
Lambda has a maximum execution timeout of 15 minutes and the
questions.explanation: Lambda's default timeout is 3 seconds, with a maximum of 15 minutes (900 seconds). Since the function runs 8 minutes but the default is only 3 seconds, it times out on every invocation. The fix is to set the timeout to at least 480 seconds. Lambda supports up to 10 GB of memory, so 3 GB is valid.

questions.q: A developer needs a Lambda function to access resources inside a private VPC (RDS, ElastiCache). After enabling VPC integration, the function can reach the VPC resources but can no longer call external AWS APIs like DynamoDB or S3. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: The VPC has no NAT Gateway or VPC Endpoints.
Lambda VPC functions cannot access AWS services; all calls must go through API Gateway
IAM execution role permissions are overridden by VPC network ACLs
The Lambda security group outbound rules block port 443
questions.explanation: When Lambda runs inside a VPC, it loses its default internet access. Without a NAT Gateway (for internet traffic) or VPC Endpoints (for private AWS service access), calls to public AWS API endpoints (DynamoDB, S3, etc.) fail. The fix is to add VPC Endpoints for the required services or route Lambda to a private subnet with a NAT Gateway. so traffic to AWS public endpoints has no route

questions.q: A developer uses Lambda with a provisioned concurrency of 100. During a traffic spike, 200 concurrent requests arrive simultaneously. What happens to the excess 100 requests?
choices: They trigger new Lambda instances from the general on-demand
They receive a 429 TooManyRequests error immediately
They are queued and processed after the first 100 complete
They are routed to the Lambda fallback region
questions.explanation: Provisioned concurrency pre-warms a fixed number of Lambda instances to eliminate cold starts. When demand exceeds provisioned concurrency, Lambda scales additional instances from the standard on-demand pool (subject to account-level concurrency limits). Only if the account limit is also reached do requests get throttled with a 429 error.

questions.q: A developer needs to call an AWS Lambda function in Account B from Account A. The calling role is in Account A. What is the MINIMUM required configuration?
choices: Enable AWS Organizations and apply a Service Control Policy allowing cross-account Lambda invocations
Create VPC peering between both accounts' default VPCs
Set up AWS PrivateLink between both accounts with a Lambda endpoint
Add a resource-based policy on the Lambda function in Account B granting invoke
questions.explanation: Lambda supports resource-based policies (like S3 bucket policies). Adding a policy on the Lambda function that allows `lambda:InvokeFunction` for the calling role's ARN (in Account A) grants cross-account access. The calling role also needs `lambda:InvokeFunction` in its identity-based policy. No VPC or PrivateLink configuration is needed for standard cross-account invocation.

questions.q: An application uses Lambda and DynamoDB Streams. The Lambda function processes stream records and occasionally throws unhandled exceptions. The developer notices Lambda is stuck retrying the same failed batch indefinitely, blocking new records from being processed. What is the BEST fix?
choices: Wrap all DynamoDB write operations in try/catch blocks
Disable DynamoDB Streams and switch to polling with an SQS FIFO queue
Increase the Lambda timeout to allow more time to process each record
Configure a bisect-on-error setting and a destination for failed records
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams with Lambda uses ordered, at-least-once delivery per shard. A failing batch blocks the shard until it succeeds or expires. The `BisectBatchOnFunctionError` setting splits a failing batch in half to isolate bad records. Combined with `DestinationConfig` pointing to SQS or EventBridge, failed individual records are preserved for debugging without blocking the stream.

questions.q: A developer needs to pass configuration values (database name, feature flags) to a Lambda function without redeploying the code. The values are non-sensitive. Which is the SIMPLEST approach?
choices: Use Lambda environment variables that can be updated via the console or CLI
Package a JSON config file inside the Lambda deployment package
Hardcode the values in the function source code and version-control them
Store values in a DynamoDB table and read them on every Lambda invocation
questions.explanation: Lambda environment variables are key-value pairs configured at the function level. Updating them via the console or API doesn't require a code redeployment — just a function update. The new values take effect on the next cold start (or warm instances may reload them depending on the implementation). This is the simplest solution for non-sensitive configuration.

questions.q: A developer has multiple Lambda functions that all share the same custom logging library and a set of third-party dependencies totalling 45 MB. Each function's deployment package is 50 MB. Which approach reduces deployment package sizes?
choices: Combine all Lambda functions into a single monolithic function to share code
Use Lambda Layers to package shared dependencies once and attach the layer to multiple functions
Store the shared libraries in S3 and download them inside the Lambda handler function on each invocation
Use Lambda@Edge to cache dependency files at CloudFront edge locations
questions.explanation: Lambda Layers are ZIP archives containing libraries, runtimes, or dependencies that you attach to functions. A layer can be shared across multiple functions and counts toward the 250 MB total unzipped size limit separately from the function code. This avoids bundling the same 45 MB of dependencies in every deployment package.

questions.q: A Lambda function occasionally receives a burst of 500 concurrent requests. The downstream RDS database can only handle 50 concurrent connections. How can a developer protect the database from connection exhaustion?
choices: Use RDS Proxy between Lambda and RDS.
Switch from RDS to DynamoDB to eliminate the connection limit problem
Set Lambda reserved concurrency to 50 to cap concurrent invocations
Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency to 50 to limit simultaneous executions
questions.explanation: RDS Proxy maintains a warm pool of database connections and multiplexes requests from many Lambda functions through a small set of connections. Hundreds of Lambda instances can share 50 or fewer actual database connections. Setting Lambda reserved concurrency to 50 would also work but would throttle your Lambda function, degrading performance. it pools and multiplexes connections from many Lambda instances

nodes.title: Amazon DynamoDB: Key Ideas
nodes.content: DynamoDB is AWS's managed NoSQL key-value store. Single-digit-ms reads at any scale, but only if your data model fits the access pattern. The exam tests partition keys, indexes, capacity modes, and the gotchas around hot partitions and item size limits.

flashcards.front: Partition key vs sort key — what do they do?
flashcards.back: Partition key (required): hashed to pick a physical partition. Items with the same PK live together. Sort key (optional): orders items within a partition; lets you query `pk = X AND sk BETWEEN a AND b`. Together they're the primary key. Pick a PK that distributes load evenly — uneven PK = hot partition = throttling.

flashcards.front: GSI vs LSI — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Local Secondary Index (LSI): different sort key on the SAME partition key, must be defined at table create, max 5. Global Secondary Index (GSI): different partition key entirely, eventually consistent, can be added later, max 20. Almost always use GSIs — LSIs have rigid constraints and are rarely worth it.

flashcards.front: On-demand vs provisioned capacity — pick a mode.
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay per request, autoscales instantly, no capacity planning, more expensive per request. Provisioned: reserve N read/write capacity units, cheaper if you know your load, can throttle on burst. Start on-demand; switch to provisioned when you've seen 2-4 weeks of traffic and the savings beat the planning effort.

flashcards.front: What's the max item size, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: 400 KB per item. Larger blobs (PDFs, images) belong in S3 with the S3 key stored in DynamoDB. Watch out for unbounded list attributes (comments, tags) that grow over time — they'll hit the cap eventually. Design for the future size, not the today size.

questions.q: A company stores user session data in DynamoDB. The table has a partition key of `userId` and receives heavy read traffic from a small set of 'celebrity' users. The team observes hot partition throttling. What is the BEST solution?
choices: Switch the partition key to a timestamp-based UUID
Increase the RCU provisioned capacity by 10x
Enable DynamoDB Auto Scaling to increase throughput automatically
Use DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) to cache popular items and
questions.explanation: DAX is an in-memory cache purpose-built for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond read performance. For 'hot key' patterns where a few items get the vast majority of reads, DAX absorbs repeated reads for the same keys, effectively eliminating hot partition throttling. Simply increasing RCU doesn't fix hot partitions — it just raises the absolute throttle ceiling.

questions.q: A developer is designing a DynamoDB schema for an e-commerce application. Each order has an `orderId` (unique) and a `customerId`. Queries must efficiently retrieve ALL orders for a given customer, sorted by order date. Which schema design BEST supports this?
choices: Partition key: customerId, Sort key: orderDate. Query using the partition key and sort key range
Partition key: customerId. Store orders as a JSON list in a single item attribute
Partition key: orderId. Scan the entire table with a FilterExpression for customerId
Partition key: orderId, Sort key: customerId. Use a Query with KeyConditionExpression
questions.explanation: Setting `customerId` as the partition key and `orderDate` as the sort key allows a single Query operation to return all orders for a customer, sorted by date, with efficient range expressions (e.g., begins_with, between). Scans are expensive and don't scale. Storing orders in a single item attribute has a 400 KB item size limit.

questions.q: A developer uses DynamoDB and needs to implement optimistic locking to prevent a lost-update problem where two processes read an item and then both write different updates. Which DynamoDB feature provides this?
choices: DynamoDB transactions with SERIALIZABLE isolation level
DynamoDB Streams with deduplication logic in Lambda
TransactWriteItems with a ConditionExpression checking the
Strongly consistent reads followed by a standard PutItem
questions.explanation: Optimistic locking in DynamoDB is implemented by adding a version number attribute to each item. When writing, use a ConditionExpression like `version = :expected_version`. If another process has already updated the item (incrementing the version), your write fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException, and you retry. TransactWriteItems lets you do this atomically across multiple items.

questions.q: A developer needs to query items from a DynamoDB table where items may NOT have the attribute being filtered. For example, retrieving all orders with `status = 'PENDING'` where some items have no `status` attribute. Which operation is correct?
choices: Use a GetItem with status as the sort key
Use a Scan with FilterExpression = 'attribute_exists(#s) AND #s
Use a Query with KeyConditionExpression = 'status = :pending'
Use a BatchGetItem with a list of all primary keys to check
questions.explanation: A full-table Scan with a FilterExpression evaluates each item after retrieval. Using `attribute_exists(#s) AND #s = :pending` (where `#s` maps to `status` via ExpressionAttributeNames) correctly handles items missing the attribute. A Query requires `status` to be a partition or sort key — it can't filter on non-key attributes alone.

questions.q: A developer uses DynamoDB and needs to update an item only if it currently exists (i.e., the item must NOT be inserted if the key doesn't exist). Which DynamoDB operation and condition achieves this?
choices: GetItem followed by PutItem in the same transaction
PutItem with ConditionExpression = 'attribute_exists(pk)'
BatchWriteItem with a conditional write flag
UpdateItem with ConditionExpression = 'attribute_exists(pk)'.
questions.explanation: UpdateItem with `ConditionExpression = 'attribute_exists(pk)'` (where `pk` is the partition key) ensures the item exists before applying the update. If the item doesn't exist, DynamoDB throws a ConditionalCheckFailedException and no write occurs. PutItem with `attribute_exists(pk)` would also work but PutItem overwrites the entire item, whereas UpdateItem only modifies specified attributes. updates only if the key already exists

questions.q: A developer needs to retrieve the 10 most recently created items from a DynamoDB table. The table's partition key is `tenantId` and sort key is `createdAt` (ISO 8601 timestamp). Which DynamoDB operation returns the 10 most recent items MOST efficiently?
choices: Query with partition key = tenantId.
GetItem 10 times with the 10 most recent known timestamps
Query without ScanIndexForward and use client-side sorting on the results
Scan the table with a Limit of 10 and a FilterExpression on createdAt
questions.explanation: DynamoDB stores items in sort key order. Setting `ScanIndexForward = false` reverses the sort order (descending by sort key). Combined with `Limit = 10`, DynamoDB returns the 10 items with the largest `createdAt` values — the most recent. This is a single efficient Query operation with no full-table scan. ScanIndexForward = false, Limit = 10 — returns the 10 most recent sorted items

questions.q: A developer receives a `TooManyRequestsException` from the DynamoDB API. CloudWatch shows the table's consumed Write Capacity Units are below the provisioned capacity. What is MOST likely causing this throttling?
choices: A hot partition
DynamoDB is throttling due to cross-region replication overhead
The Lambda function's IAM role has exceeded its API rate limit
The table has reached its maximum item count limit
questions.explanation: DynamoDB distributes data across partitions. Each partition has a maximum throughput (3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU). Even if total table WCU is below provisioned capacity, if writes are concentrated on a few partition keys (hot partitions), those partitions get throttled individually. The solution is to design a better partition key with higher cardinality to distribute writes evenly. exceeding that partition's throughput limit

nodes.title: Azure API Management (AZ-204 / AZ-305): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Azure API Management (APIM) is a managed gateway layer that sits in front of backend APIs. AZ-204 tests the four policy sections (inbound, backend, outbound, on-error) that transform and govern requests, the rate-limiting and JWT-validation policies, response caching, and the developer portal for external API consumers.

flashcards.front: APIM policy sections — what runs in each of the four phases?
flashcards.back: Inbound: runs first on the request before it reaches the backend — authentication (validate-jwt), rate limiting (rate-limit-by-key), request transformation (set-header, rewrite-uri), IP filtering. Backend: controls how the gateway calls the backend — retry policy, circuit breaker, load balancing between backends. Outbound: transforms the response before returning to the caller — add/remove headers, mask sensitive fields, inject CORS headers. On-error: handles exceptions — return custom error responses, log diagnostics.

flashcards.front: rate-limit-by-key policy — how does it work?
flashcards.back: Limits the number of calls per key (subscription, IP, JWT claim) within a time window. Example: `<rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" />` limits each subscriber to 100 calls per 60 seconds. Returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header when exceeded. Use `quota-by-key` for soft monthly caps (reset monthly, not per second). These are the primary monetization / abuse-prevention levers in APIM.

flashcards.front: validate-jwt policy — what does it verify?
flashcards.back: Validates a Bearer JWT in the Authorization header (or a custom header/query param). Checks signature against a specified JWKS URI or symmetric key, verifies iss (issuer), aud (audience), exp (expiry), and nbf (not before). Can also require specific claims to be present. On failure, returns HTTP 401 without forwarding to the backend. This centralizes auth at the gateway so individual backends don't need to implement JWT validation.

flashcards.front: APIM developer portal — what is it for?
flashcards.back: An auto-generated, customizable website where external developers discover, read documentation for, and subscribe to your APIs. It shows OpenAPI specs rendered as interactive try-it-out pages, subscription key management, and usage analytics. Consumers sign up, get an API key (subscription key), and test calls from the portal. It separates the developer onboarding experience from the API implementation — a standard requirement for public or partner APIs.

questions.q: A developer needs to expose a REST API that invokes Lambda functions. The API must cache responses for 5 minutes per unique query string parameter combination. Which feature enables this?
choices: ElastiCache for Memcached placed between API Gateway and Lambda
Lambda reserved concurrency with response caching enabled
API Gateway stage-level caching with cache key set to include query
CloudFront in front of API Gateway with TTL set to 300 seconds
questions.explanation: API Gateway has a built-in response cache at the stage level. You enable it per stage, set a TTL (up to 3600s), and configure which request parameters (query strings, headers, path variables) are included in the cache key. This avoids invoking Lambda for identical repeated requests within the TTL window.

questions.q: A developer implements a Cognito-protected REST API in API Gateway. The JWT from Cognito User Pools must be validated before routing to the backend. Which integration achieves this with the LEAST custom code?
choices: Use an API Gateway resource policy to allow only authenticated Cognito IP addresses
Place CloudFront in front of API Gateway and configure a CloudFront function for token validation
Write a Lambda authorizer that manually validates the JWT signature using the Cognito JWKS endpoint
Configure a Cognito User Pool Authorizer directly in API Gateway — it validates the JWT natively
questions.explanation: API Gateway has a native Cognito User Pool Authorizer integration. You configure it with the User Pool ARN and it automatically validates the JWT (issuer, signature, expiry, audience) using Cognito's JWKS endpoint. No custom Lambda code is required. The validated claims are forwarded to the backend in `$context.authorizer.claims`.

questions.q: A developer builds an API Gateway REST API with Lambda proxy integration. The frontend receives HTTP 502 errors for some requests. The Lambda function logs show it completed successfully. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: API Gateway is unable to parse the Lambda function's CloudWatch logs
API Gateway is throttling requests due to exceeding the burst limit
The Lambda function is not returning a properly formatted response object
The Lambda function exceeded its timeout before returning
questions.explanation: With Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway expects the Lambda function to return a specific JSON structure: `{"statusCode": 200, "headers": {}, "body": "..."}`. If the Lambda returns an invalid format (wrong field names, missing statusCode, unserializable body), API Gateway returns a 502 Bad Gateway error. The function itself succeeds — the failure is in the response serialization. headers, and body

questions.q: A developer is building a web application that needs to support thousands of concurrent WebSocket connections for real-time notifications. The backend is serverless. Which AWS service handles persistent WebSocket connections natively without managing servers?
choices: API Gateway HTTP API with long-polling Lambda functions
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with WebSocket SDK clients
Application Load Balancer WebSocket listener with Lambda targets
API Gateway WebSocket API with Lambda integration for connect.
questions.explanation: API Gateway WebSocket APIs maintain persistent WebSocket connections on behalf of your backend. Lambda functions handle `$connect`, `$disconnect`, and custom message routes. The backend can push messages back to connected clients using the API Gateway Management API (`POST /@connections/{connectionId}`). This is fully serverless — no EC2 or WebSocket servers to manage. disconnect, and message routes

questions.q: A developer is implementing an API Gateway Lambda authorizer (custom authorizer). The Lambda function validates a custom token and returns an IAM policy. To avoid invoking the authorizer Lambda on every request, which feature should the developer enable?
choices: Lambda provisioned concurrency to keep the authorizer warm
Lambda@Edge to cache authorization decisions at edge locations
API Gateway authorizer result caching with a TTL.
CloudFront caching in front of API Gateway to cache authorization headers
questions.explanation: API Gateway Lambda authorizers support result caching. When enabled, the IAM policy returned by the authorizer is cached by the identity source (e.g., the token value) for a configurable TTL (up to 3600 seconds). Subsequent requests with the same token reuse the cached policy without invoking the authorizer Lambda, reducing latency and cost. the IAM policy is cached per token/identity source

nodes.title: AWS CloudFormation: Key Ideas
nodes.content: CloudFormation is AWS's native IaC service — declarative YAML/JSON templates that describe stacks of AWS resources. The control plane handles ordering, rollback on failure, and drift detection. The exam tests intrinsic functions, change sets, and stack lifecycle.

flashcards.front: What's a change set?
flashcards.back: A preview of what would happen if you applied an updated template. Lists adds, modifies, replaces (resources that must be destroyed and recreated). Lets you spot dangerous changes (replacing your prod RDS!) before executing. Always use change sets in production; never `update-stack` blind.

flashcards.front: When is a resource replaced vs updated in place?
flashcards.back: Depends on the property changed. Some properties (instance type) update in place. Others (security group name, RDS engine version major) require replacement: CFN creates a new resource, updates references, then deletes the old. Replacement = downtime + possible data loss. Read the docs before changing names or immutable IDs.

flashcards.front: Stack policy — what does it protect?
flashcards.back: A JSON document attached to a stack that says 'these resource updates are NOT allowed during stack update'. Typical use: lock the prod database resource so an accidental rerun of `update-stack` can't drop it. Default policy: everything mutable; you opt in to lock specific logical IDs.

flashcards.front: Nested stacks vs cross-stack references.
flashcards.back: Nested: parent template instantiates child templates as `AWS::CloudFormation::Stack` resources — tight coupling, one deploy unit. Cross-stack: stack A exports an output, stack B imports it via `Fn::ImportValue` — loose coupling, independent lifecycles. Pick nested for reusable patterns, cross-stack for shared infra (VPC) referenced by many apps.

questions.q: A developer uses CloudFormation to manage infrastructure. A stack update causes an EC2 instance replacement, which is a disruptive change. The developer wants to preview exactly which resources will be replaced BEFORE applying the change. Which CloudFormation feature provides this?
choices: CloudFormation Change Sets.
CloudTrail to log all API calls made by CloudFormation
AWS Config to track infrastructure change history
CloudFormation Drift Detection to compare current state with template
questions.explanation: CloudFormation Change Sets show you the exact changes (Add, Modify, Remove) and for modified resources whether they will be updated in-place or replaced (Replacement: True). You review the change set and execute it only when satisfied. This prevents surprise disruptions from stack updates. create a change set to preview modifications, replacements, and additions before execution

questions.q: A developer deploys a CloudFormation stack but the stack creation fails. CloudFormation rolls back automatically. The developer needs to investigate the root cause. Where should they look FIRST?
choices: The CloudFormation stack's Events tab.
AWS CloudTrail logs for all API calls made during deployment
Amazon Inspector findings for the failed resources
AWS Config timeline for each resource that failed
questions.explanation: The CloudFormation stack Events tab is the first place to look. It shows a chronological list of resource creation/update events with status (CREATE_FAILED, etc.) and the reason message from the underlying service (e.g., 'IAM role does not have permission to...' or 'Value is not valid'). This pinpoints exactly which resource failed and why. it shows each resource action and the specific failure reason

questions.q: A developer creates a CloudFormation template that includes a custom resource backed by a Lambda function. The Lambda function must respond to CloudFormation during stack creation or the stack will time out. What must the Lambda function do to signal CloudFormation?
choices: Return a CloudFormation-formatted JSON response from the Lambda handler function
Send an HTTP PUT request to the pre-signed S3 URL provided in the CloudFormation event's
Publish a success message to the SNS topic ARN included in the CloudFormation event
Write a success file to the S3 bucket specified by the CloudFormation StackId
questions.explanation: CloudFormation custom resources work via a response URL pattern. CloudFormation sends an event to Lambda containing a `ResponseURL` (a pre-signed S3 URL). The Lambda function must PUT a JSON response object (with Status: SUCCESS/FAILED, PhysicalResourceId, and optional Data) to that URL. If it doesn't, the custom resource waits until it times out (up to 1 hour) and the stack fails.

questions.q: A developer writes a CloudFormation template that creates an S3 bucket and exports its name. A second stack imports that bucket name using `Fn::ImportValue`. After both stacks are deployed, the developer tries to update the first stack to change the bucket name but gets an error. Why?
choices: The `Fn::ImportValue` function creates a hard dependency that requires both stacks to be updated simultaneously
Exported values in CloudFormation are immutable — you must delete and recreate the stack
S3 bucket names cannot be changed after creation regardless of CloudFormation
CloudFormation prevents deletion or modification of exports that are actively referenced by other stacks
questions.explanation: CloudFormation cross-stack references create a dependency lock. If Stack B imports an export from Stack A, CloudFormation prevents you from modifying or deleting that export (or the resource it references) in Stack A until Stack B is updated or deleted. This protects against breaking dependent stacks. To update, you must first remove the import from Stack B.

questions.q: A developer creates a CloudFormation stack with a DeletionPolicy of `Retain` on an RDS instance. When the developer deletes the stack, what happens to the RDS instance?
choices: The RDS instance is moved to a suspended state for 30 days before permanent deletion
The RDS instance is removed from the CloudFormation stack but continues to exist in the AWS account
CloudFormation deletes the RDS instance and creates a final snapshot before deletion
CloudFormation refuses to delete the stack until the DeletionPolicy is removed
questions.explanation: The `DeletionPolicy: Retain` attribute tells CloudFormation to keep the resource when the stack is deleted. The resource is removed from CloudFormation management (no longer in the stack state) but continues to exist in your AWS account with all its data. You must delete it manually after stack deletion. This is commonly used for databases to prevent accidental data loss.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An application uses Amazon SQS as a buffer between a producer service and Lambda consumers. After a deployment, you notice the same messages are being processed multiple times, causing duplicate charges. What setting should you check FIRST?
choices: Enable SQS FIFO queue to guarantee exactly-once processing
Increase the Lambda concurrency limit to match SQS throughput
Set the Lambda dead letter queue target to an S3 bucket
Extend the SQS visibility timeout to be longer than the maximum
questions.explanation: If the visibility timeout is shorter than the Lambda function's actual processing time, SQS makes the message visible again (assuming the consumer died) and another Lambda instance picks it up — causing duplicates. The fix is to set the visibility timeout to at least 6x the function's timeout. Making your Lambda idempotent is also best practice.

questions.q: A company processes financial transactions using Lambda and SQS. Occasionally Lambda fails to process a message after 3 retries. The team wants failed messages preserved for manual review without losing them. What is the CORRECT configuration?
choices: Enable SQS long polling with a 20-second wait time
Configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) on the SQS queue and
Set the Lambda event source mapping batch size to 1
Set the SQS queue retention period to 14 days
questions.explanation: A Dead Letter Queue receives messages that fail processing after `maxReceiveCount` delivery attempts. Setting maxReceiveCount to 3 means after 3 failed Lambda invocations, SQS moves the message to the DLQ where it stays for manual inspection and replay. This prevents message loss while isolating poison-pill messages.

questions.q: A Lambda function processes messages from an SQS queue. During testing, the developer notices all messages are processed twice. The Lambda function takes 45 seconds to process each message. The SQS visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What should the developer do?
choices: Increase the SQS visibility timeout to be greater than the Lambda function's
Add deduplication logic inside the Lambda function using a DynamoDB table
Reduce the Lambda batch size to 1 to prevent parallel processing
Enable SQS FIFO queue to guarantee exactly-once processing
questions.explanation: When the SQS visibility timeout (30s) is shorter than the Lambda processing time (45s), the message becomes visible again before Lambda finishes, causing SQS to deliver it to another consumer. Setting the visibility timeout to at least 6× the function timeout (AWS recommendation) — or at minimum longer than 45 seconds — prevents premature re-delivery.

questions.q: A development team uses Elastic Beanstalk to deploy a Node.js application. During a new deployment, the team wants ZERO downtime and wants to test the new version before making it the primary version. Which deployment policy meets these requirements?
choices: Rolling with additional batch — adds new instances before removing old ones
Blue/Green — deploy to a separate environment and swap CNAMEs after validation
All at once — fastest but causes downtime
Immutable — deploys to a fresh set of instances; swap to production only after health check passes
questions.explanation: Blue/Green deployment in Elastic Beanstalk creates a completely separate environment with the new version. After validating the green environment, you swap environment URLs (CNAME swap) to route production traffic to it. The old blue environment remains intact for instant rollback. Immutable is also zero-downtime but doesn't preserve the old environment for easy rollback as a fully separate testable stack.

questions.q: A developer uses Elastic Beanstalk and needs to install a custom package (e.g., ImageMagick) on the EC2 instances during deployment. The package is not in the standard yum repository. Which Elastic Beanstalk configuration mechanism handles this?
choices: Create a `.ebextensions` configuration file with a `commands` or `packages`
Modify the Elastic Beanstalk platform configuration via the Elastic Beanstalk console
Add a `packages` key to the Elastic Beanstalk environment variables
Create a custom AMI with the package pre-installed and reference it in the launch configuration
questions.explanation: `.ebextensions` YAML files (placed in a `.ebextensions/` directory in your deployment package) are Elastic Beanstalk's customization mechanism. The `commands` section runs shell commands, `packages` installs from yum/apt, and `files` creates configuration files. They run during instance provisioning before the application starts. Creating a custom AMI would also work but adds significant maintenance overhead.

questions.q: An Elastic Beanstalk application uses an RDS database. The developer wants to ensure the database is NOT deleted when the Elastic Beanstalk environment is terminated. What is the BEST approach?
choices: Use an Elastic Beanstalk saved configuration to preserve the RDS settings after termination
Enable RDS deletion protection in the Elastic Beanstalk environment configuration
Create the RDS instance outside of Elastic Beanstalk (decoupled) and pass the connection
Enable Elastic Beanstalk environment termination protection
questions.explanation: When RDS is created inside an Elastic Beanstalk environment, it's tied to the environment lifecycle — deleting the environment deletes the database. The best practice is to create RDS independently (outside Elastic Beanstalk) and inject the endpoint and credentials as environment variables. This decouples the database lifecycle from the application environment.

questions.q: A developer uses AWS X-Ray to trace requests through an application. The team wants to add business-specific metadata (like `userId` and `orderId`) to traces for filtering and grouping in the X-Ray console. Which X-Ray concept is used for indexed, searchable values?
choices: Subsegments — used to track downstream calls to databases or HTTP endpoints
Sampling rules — configure which percentage of requests get traced
Annotations
Metadata — key-value pairs added to segments for any arbitrary data
questions.explanation: X-Ray Annotations are key-value pairs (string, number, boolean) that X-Ray indexes. You can use them in filter expressions in the X-Ray console to find traces by specific annotation values (e.g., `annotation.userId = "user-123"`). Metadata is for non-indexed, non-searchable data — it's stored in traces but can't be used in filter expressions.

questions.q: A developer wants to trace Lambda function calls and all downstream AWS SDK calls (DynamoDB, S3) using AWS X-Ray. What is the MINIMUM change required in the Lambda function?
choices: Enable X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda function and instrument the AWS SDK using the X-Ray
Enable CloudWatch ServiceLens — it automatically instruments Lambda functions
Add a custom X-Ray segment in every handler function manually
Install the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry as a Lambda layer and add a OTEL_EXPORTER environment variable
questions.explanation: Enabling Active Tracing on the Lambda function makes Lambda send trace segments to X-Ray for the function itself. To also trace downstream AWS SDK calls (DynamoDB, S3, etc.), wrap the SDK client with the X-Ray SDK: `AWSXRay.captureAWSv3Client(new DynamoDBClient({}))`. This automatically creates subsegments for each downstream call with timing and response data.
